facts.claim: As at November 2026, the Federal Register of Legislation lists the current compilation of the Marriage Act 1961 (No. 12, 1961) as C2026C00129, compilation 34, dated 28 March 2026, administered by the Attorney-General's Department; Part IV Division 2 includes section 45 'Form of ceremony' and section 46 'Certain authorised celebrants to explain nature of marriage relationship'.

Marriage Act 1961 (Cth), as reproduced on AustLII (read 19 November 2026): s45(1): where a marriage is solemnised by an authorised celebrant who is a minister of religion, it may be solemnised according to any form and ceremony recognised as sufficient for the purpose by the religious body or organisation of which he or she is a minister.

Marriage Act 1961 (Cth), as reproduced on AustLII (read 19 November 2026): s45(2): where a marriage is solemnised by an authorised celebrant who is not a minister of religion, it is sufficient if each of the parties says to the other, in the presence of the authorised celebrant and the witnesses, the words: 'I call upon the persons here present to witness that I, A.B. (or C.D.), take thee, C.D. (or A.B.), to be my lawful wedded wife (or husband, or spouse)'; or words to that effect.

Marriage Act 1961 (Cth), as reproduced on AustLII (read 19 November 2026): s46(1): before a marriage is solemnised by an authorised celebrant who is not a minister of religion of a recognised denomination, the celebrant shall say to the parties, in the presence of the witnesses, the words: 'I am duly authorised by law to solemnise marriages according to law. Before you are joined in marriage in my presence and in the presence of these witnesses, I am to remind you of the solemn and binding nature of the relationship into which you are now about to enter. Marriage, according to law in Australia, is the union of 2 people to the exclusion of all others, voluntarily entered into for life.'; or words to that effect.

Marriage Act 1961 (Cth), as reproduced on AustLII (read 19 November 2026): s46(2): the Minister may exempt certain celebrants authorised under subsection 39(2) from s46(1) where satisfied their form of ceremony sufficiently states the nature and obligations of marriage.

As at November 2026, smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (last updated 18 August 2026): you can't register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if valid where it happened and valid under Australian law had it occurred in Australia; talk to a lawyer to confirm. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

facts.claim: As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): to get married in Australia you must, among other things, 'give a notice of intended marriage form to an authorised marriage celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before your wedding' and 'be married by an authorised marriage celebrant'. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): under 'Before you get married': 'complete a notice of intended marriage form' and 'give it to an authorised marriage celebrant at least 1 month (but not more than 18 months) before your wedding. Ask your authorised marriage celebrant if you need help with the form.' The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): 'If there is less than 1 month until your wedding, talk to your authorised marriage celebrant. You may be able to get married if a prescribed authority approves it.' Reasons listed for getting married in less than 1 month: employment-related or travel commitments; wedding or celebration arrangements; medical reasons; legal proceedings; error in giving notice. The page links 'prescribed authority' to https://marriage.ag.gov.au/stateofficers/authorities (not read in this round). The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

The Attorney-General's Department's Notice of Intended Marriage publication page (last updated 22 December 2022) says section 42 of the Marriage Act 1961 requires that a marriage shall not be solemnised unless a notice in writing of the intended marriage (this form) is given to the authorised celebrant solemnising the marriage. The form is downloadable as PDF and DOCX.

AGD: the requirements for authorised witnesses remain unchanged and location-dependent. If the couple is in Australia, the person remotely witnessing the NOIM (which can include an authorised celebrant) must also be in Australia. If the couple is outside Australia, the authorised witness (which cannot be a celebrant) must also be outside Australia. A NOIM for a person or couple outside Australia cannot be witnessed online.

Marriage Act 1961 (Federal Register of Legislation, latest compilation dated 28 March 2026, read live 13 November 2026; table of contents only, section text not returned): Part IV Division 2 includes s 41 'Marriages to be solemnised by authorised celebrant', s 42 'Notice to be given and declaration made', s 42A 'Commissioner of Australian Federal Police or approved authority may issue special notice', s 42B 'Authorised celebrant must physically meet each party to intended marriage separately', s 44 'Witnesses', and s 104 'Giving defective notice etc.' (offence). The Act is administered by the Attorney-General's Department.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): overseas marriages cannot be performed by an Australian-authorised marriage celebrant and cannot be registered in Australia. An overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was a valid marriage in the overseas country and would have been a valid marriage here. Smartraveller has information on getting married overseas. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

facts.claim: [Copied from same-sex-marriage-greece 03-source-pack fact_106, same source and date.] As at November 2026, Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (last updated 18/08/2026, read live 12 November 2026): some countries ask you to prove you aren't already married; the most common documents are a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) and certificates from a registry of births, deaths and marriages; the country may have more rules (for example a residence period); 'We can't tell you what you will need'; contact your destination's embassy or consulate. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

[Copied from same-sex-marriage-greece 03-source-pack fact_107, same source and date.] As at November 2026, Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (read live 12 November 2026): your registry of births, deaths and marriages can give a statement that there's no record you have been married before, a Single Status certificate or a No Record Result certificate; local authorities may also ask for divorce papers, the death certificate of a deceased spouse, and your original birth certificate and passport.

[Copied from same-sex-marriage-greece 03-source-pack fact_115 (originally mykonos-wedding part-1 fact_101), same source and date.] As at November 2026, Smartraveller (read live 11 November 2026) says DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia, but some local authorities only accept CNIs issued in their country, so ask the destination's embassy or consulate whether you need a CNI, whether you can get it in Australia, and whether it also needs an authentication or apostille. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Get married' page (read live 13 November 2026; page metadata updated 13 June 2024): on the wedding day 3 marriage certificates must be signed by the couple, the authorised celebrant and 2 witnesses over 18. The celebrant gives the couple a ceremonial certificate of marriage on the day, then must, within 14 days of the marriage, submit the marriage paperwork to the registry of births, deaths and marriages in the state or territory where the marriage took place.

insider_details.detail: For couples abroad who want the legal paperwork simple, a common route is a short legal marriage in Australia with an authorised celebrant, with the Notice of Intended Marriage lodged at least 1 month and no more than 18 months ahead, then the full ceremony overseas as a symbolic ceremony. Plan the NOIM before you fly, because a NOIM given from outside Australia cannot be witnessed online and the witness cannot be a celebrant.

A legal wedding abroad needs paperwork from Australia that can take time to gather: a Certificate of No Impediment, registry certificates and sometimes an apostille, and some destinations only accept a CNI issued locally. Ask the destination's embassy or consulate early, because Smartraveller says it cannot tell you what you will need.
An overseas marriage cannot be registered in Australia, so the foreign certificate is your proof of marriage. Keep it safe and check with your state registry before relying on it for a name change.

An Australian-authorised celebrant cannot perform a legal marriage overseas, so if an Australian celebrant travels with you, the ceremony abroad is symbolic unless a local legal process is also completed.

In a legal Australian ceremony with a civil celebrant, the Act sets the words the celebrant must say (s46(1)) and the words each of you must say to the other (s45(2)), 'or words to that effect'. A symbolic ceremony abroad has no such required wording, so it can be shaped however you like. Phrase this as general information as at November 2026, not legal advice.
